name: Gyaru

influenced_by: American pop culture imagery (California beach and glamour tropes), reinterpreted through a specifically Japanese lens
a rejection of traditional Japanese standards of feminine modesty

media.title: Egg magazine (1995–2014, relaunched later)
media.note: the main print record of the gyaru scene's many sub-styles

reacts_against: the pale skin, quiet demeanor and restrained dress long held up as the ideal for young Japanese women, inverting nearly every element of it on purpose.
article: Gyaru (a Japanese rendering of the English "gal") emerged in the 1990s as young Japanese women built a look almost point-for-point opposed to the era's conventional femininity: deliberately tanned skin instead of the prized pale complexion, bleached and heavily styled hair, dramatic false-lash makeup, loud instead of quiet self-presentation. The scene splintered into distinct, well-documented sub-styles tracked closely by magazines like Egg — ganguro pushed the tan and contrast furthest, himegyaru ("princess gyaru") added pastel, doll-like glamour, and several other named variants each carried their own specific makeup and silhouette rules. Academic and journalistic accounts of gyaru culture consistently frame it as a form of visible rebellion against expectations of restraint and modesty placed on young women, closer in spirit to punk's confrontational self-presentation than to a simple fashion trend, even though its specific visual vocabulary (tan, lashes, platform boots) looks nothing like Western punk.

findings: mostly muted — about 75% of the measured color is low-saturation (greys, dusty tones)
measured.caveat: Colors measured from Aesthetics Wiki images as photographed and displayed on screen; actual materials vary, and screen colors are approximate.
